en: You might remember that slide. I talked
about the nature of an algorithm, which you
should detect, a few lectures ago. It is
important that you don't always have to
manually count operations, but that you have
a couple of things to look for, like loops
and then the exit condition or the change of
the iterator in the loop, so that you're
quickly able to identify the Big O notation,
the time complexity of an algorithm.
Now we learned about logarithmic time.
There, the runtime does grow, but it doesn't
grow at a similar pace as it does with
linear time complexity.
Linear time complexity means that if you add
1 to n,
the runtime also takes 1 unit longer.
Logarithmic time complexity simply means
that if you add 1 to n,
the runtime takes longer but it doesn't grow
linearly. The time it might take longer is a
very small fraction that it takes longer. So
there is no linear relation between n and
the increase in runtime.
And you typically have such algorithms
if you have an algorithm
where you
have some kind of logic, for example, inside
of a loop where the number, where n is split
into smaller chunks. So that's something you
might want to look for. Like in this case,
we're splitting the number we're going
through by 2 in every iteration.
Keep in mind that divided number is part of
our loop condition here. So if we change the
divided number, we of course affect the
number of iterations we need since the
number has a direct impact on the number of
iterations.
And if we split it by 2 in every iteration,
it's of course relatively easy to see that
we're not dealing with a linear time
complexity here
because big numbers quickly become very
small
if we divide them by 2 in every iteration.
And if we then use that divided number in
our loop condition, well, we're certainly
only dealing with a relatively small amount
of iterations.
So if you have something like this where you
split your exit condition number or your
input number into smaller chunks in every
iteration,
then you're typically dealing with
logarithmic time.
Because if you split a number, even a big
number becomes a small number relatively
quickly. So therefore, things like that are
something you should watch out for when
you're looking at an algorithm because
splitting your number, splitting your data
you're running your operation on into
smaller chunks
as part of a loop is a clear indicator that
you're having logarithmic time complexity.
